technique: the second person — how 'you' pulls the reader into the room
lesson:
Today we work on one thing: the second person. That means the poem uses the word "you" to speak straight to the listener, as if you are the one doing the actions.

Hear where it does this. "your thumb knows the give of it before you're awake." Then "Rain's coming — you can feel it in the handles." Then "only your own two hands can finish today."

This works because when the poem says "you," your brain tries it out. You put yourself at that door. You feel the cold latch, because it says your thumb, not someone else's. So the poem stops being a report and becomes something happening to you.

Try this: write a few lines about a morning task, and use "you" and "your" instead of "I" or "he."

The second time through, listen for how all that "you" sets up the two words at the end, "So — up!"

Here is the poem.
poem:
The latch on the barn door's cold enough to bite,
a little rough where the paint has worn to iron,
and your thumb knows the give of it before you're awake,
that small resistance, then the swing and the smell
of straw and must and the night's held damp inside.
Rain's coming — you can feel it in the handles,
the way they sweat, the way the tools go heavy.
There's a rack to shift before the frost sets hard,
pots to sink and twist down to the rim,
and the far ridge gone the color of banked coals.
You stand a moment, breath loose on the air,
the whole gray weight of the day laid out and waiting.

There's a few things waiting that only your own two hands can finish today.

So — up!
